Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the data patterns:

## Example 1 (2024-10-28)
- Model forecasts are generally lower than true outcomes
- At day 1: Model 66.27 vs True 66.40 (off by -0.13)
- At day 9: Model 65.89 vs True 68.02 (off by -2.13) - significant undershoot
- At day 18: Model 63.85 vs True 67.34 (off by -3.49) - major undershoot

## Example 2 (2024-10-15)
- Similar pattern - model forecasts are too low
- Day 1: Model 65.37 vs True 65.09 (off by +0.28, this is actually higher)
- Day 9: Model 65.75 vs True 66.40 (off by -0.65)
- Day 18: Model 64.50 vs True 67.86 (off by -3.36)

## Example 3 (2024-10-21)
- Day 1: Model 61.75 vs True 61.76 (very close)
- Day 9: Model 62.03 vs True 68.02 (off by -5.99) - massive undershoot
- Day 18: Model 61.87 vs True 67.63 (off by -5.76)

## Example 4 (2024-10-22)
- Day 1: Model 61.95 vs True 62.25 (off by -0.30)
- Day 9: Model 61.76 vs True 63.87 (off by -2.11)
- Day 18: Model 62.91 vs True 67.63 (off by -4.72)

## Example 5 (2024-10-18)


I notice a consistent pattern of model forecasts being 2-4 units lower than true outcomes, particularly in the early days of the projection. The deviations seem to follow a systematic downward bias, with the largest differences occurring around day 9 and day 18.
